speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also the body which the Government is ultimately accountable to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, while Singapore has a strong reputation for strong Government, can we equally say that we have a strong Parliament?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, we talk a lot a lot about the executive but Parliamentary work is the reason why voters put Members in this House.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Inter-Parliamentary Union, of which our Parliament is a member, states that parliaments must be representative, open and transparent, accessible, accountable and effective.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It notes that, "Parliaments are constantly evolving in order to meet new challenges and expectations and crucially that parliaments can always improve, like democracy itself." Thus, the Speaker presides over the Sittings of the House and enforces rules prescribed in the Standing Orders of Parliament and during Sittings, is responsible for regulating and enforcing the rules of debate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In order to do so, it is imperative that the Speaker is and is seen to be impartial at all times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is the reason why the Speaker does not take part in debates and thus the saying that the Speaker may do anything except speak.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many jurisdictions have enshrined the principle of the Speaker's impartiality in their rules.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some ways in which jurisdictions have approached this, include having the Speaker not take part in votes in the House, as is the case of Germany's Bundestag retaining party membership, but no longer participating in national party caucuses and also, in the case of the Speaker of the House of Commons in Canada.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Or even a system of rotation and the election of a Speaker or amongst their deputies between major parties like we see in countries like Austria.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Speaker as presiding officer is also responsible for ensuring that Standing Orders are followed to ensure that public business is conducted in a decent and orderly manner, balancing the government of the day's need to get its business through Parliament and the oppositions' responsibility to debate and scrutinise that business.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Speaker may thus be called upon to make rulings and decisions on points of order from time to time and it will be helpful for these to serve as precedents to govern future proceedings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What advisories are helpful, having easy access to past Speaker's rulings can also help Members better understand and thus abide by the Standing Orders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, on why an accessible Parliament is important.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In order for Parliament to properly represent and hold the respect of our people, it must not be seen as a cold tower which operates independently and heedlessly of our constituents' everyday lives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our people must believe that Parliament is a place where the people's concerns are debated and for their voices to be heard.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To build respect for Parliament as a lynchpin of our democracy, we have to ensure that as much as possible, our policy, law-making and accountability processes flow through our Parliament first and foremost; and the chosen means to discuss important matters of public interest in Parliament, also matters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In short, having members of the public, experts and different interest groups provide evidence, like was the case during the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods, can ensure more voices are heard and lead to interested parties being able to watch the proceedings and thus understand the complexity of the issues being considered.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have to keep working to keep Parliament as accessible to our people as possible with increased openness; reduced secrecy – whether perceived or real – to promote the man in the street's understanding of the actual process of legislating and making queries of how their taxpayer dollars are being spent.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Where information is shared, it has to be on the basis of full disclosure unless circumstances dictate otherwise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Maintaining the principle of parliamentary transparency and openness can only encourage and advance more participatory democracy and better governance, and I hope that all of us here will play our part in enabling this to happen in a world that is getting increasingly unpredictable and volatile.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But none of these is specific to individual Ministries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is quite unlike many other legislatures around the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The United Kingdom's (UK’s) House of Commons, for example, has Select Committees for every government department, like Defence, Home Affairs and Transport, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Australia's parliament has House Standing Committees on Health, Aged Care and Sport and on Employment, Education and Training, among others.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These Select Committees examine each Ministry's policies, spending and administration.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are empowered to inquire into and report on any matter referred to them by the House or Minister.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The committees may call in subject matter experts to give testimony and answer questions from members that can inform their considerations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Select Committees also provide a platform for members of parliament (MPs) to better understand each other's positions and that of the government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The government may share in confidence with committees information that shapes its policy stances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The committees can discuss legislation or major policy changes before they are officially tabled so that there is more room to work out, compromises before each party takes its position publicly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: After a thorough scrutiny of legislation and policies, the Select Committees can make recommendations to parliament before Bills and Motions are debated and voted on by all MPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This process will lead to more informed and constructive debate and better decision making in parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The committees thus help to contribute to more effective governance, build political consensus and strengthen national unity.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: "It will be harder and harder to attract good people" "…it is a very serious problem".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These were comments made by the Prime Minister in the book "The History of the PAP".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The PAP has, for a long time, been very candid about the challenges it faces convincing good people to enter politics.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On the other side of the aisle, the Leader of the Opposition has also said that the Workers' Party's (WP's) search for candidates was always an ongoing process.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The quality of the Members in this House is of paramount importance.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Cabinet is drawn from amongst MPs and legislative debate is critical to articulate views on the ground, for transparency and accountability and to shape public opinion.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But over the years, it is not only the demands on MPs that have grown, but also their exposure to toxic social media and encroachments on their private lives.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: How do we continue to attract the very best into Parliament?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, I think that we need to be realistic about what makes a good politician.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Do we expect that our politicians will be flawless individuals; who had hardly set a wrong foot; and who had not and will not make mistakes or missteps along the way.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is an impossibly high bar that will deter many good candidates from joining.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What Singaporeans expect is influenced by how parties position themselves and their candidates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, to a certain extent, if Singaporeans develop unrealistic expectations of their MPs, the problem is somewhat self-made by the parties themselves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This having been said, the bar of course must be set very high – not impossibly high – but very high because these are our national leaders after all.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I think this is also what is of critical importance to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: MPs, like everyone else, have flaws, fears and doubts and will make mistakes from time to time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I think a candidate who admits and owns these mistakes and who shows he has learnt from them and has become a better person, can still be a good candidate as long as they meet the cardinal criteria.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We can draw wisdom from an ancient Chinese idiom on governance: clear waters do not have any fish.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A person who is perfect and devoid of failings will have a sterile mind and hold no interesting or useful ideas or contributions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Flaws, the impurities in the water, are what underpin character and experience.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It grants a person empathy that allows him to connect with and to understand others.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, there are some impurities that are in fact, poisons.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such persons should be weeded out as best as possible by each party's vetting processes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But otherwise, persons who have a passion to serve and who are competent, should step up to serve.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They should not be deterred by an impossibly high bar set by party and public expectations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My second point is on the use of social media.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The nastiness hurled at MPs on social media, often at a personal level, is something that, sadly, MPs and future MPs must come to accept.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is an inevitable outcome of an open society that is highly connected to the internet and a populace that is opinionated.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are a lot of complaints about MPs online.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are those that surface real concerns, but a lot of it is griping and sniping.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Someone approached me in July last year on a very urgent family matter.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Seeing that this person was a resident in Minister of State Alvin Tan's constituency, I asked him if he could help look into it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On the day that I referred the matter to the Minister of State, he was moving a Bill and the Sitting ended at close to 9.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Despite that, the Minister of State rushed down to meet the resident and spent quite a bit of time with them to understand their situation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He helped to coordinate with the relevant agency over the next few days and sorted the matter out.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I told the resident later – well, looks like he did a good job.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And I have no doubt that there are many examples of the good work and effort our MPs, both ruling party and opposition, put in to serve their constituents.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, how do we better showcase the good work that our MPs do without an MP being accused of "ownself praise ownself"?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Residents can consider posting such positive accounts online, akin to a Google review.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But for many such cases, residents may not want to draw attention to their situations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, grassroots organisations could consider highlighting positive cases with the consent of the resident and properly anonymised, like my anecdote earlier.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These would serve to show how MPs can help their constituents, as well as a form of accountability that their MPs are actually working and getting things done for them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think that our MPs do what they do to get praise.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is not because they have something to hide, but it is simply because many aspects of private life are just not anyone else's business.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In many other countries, this has been taken to an extreme; with the media and even government agencies probing into politicians' lives on things that have nothing to do with their official duties and often, with political intent or an intent to embarrass.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As an absolute minimum, MPs' family members must be out of bounds in the political arena.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many new candidates would be in their 30s and 40s, with families and young children.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Subjecting their families to the public glare would be foremost in their minds and could be the deal breaker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, it is not possible to prevent anonymous online vigilantes from making claims or spreading rumours about MPs' family members.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But it is possible for political parties, whether currently represented in Parliament or otherwise, to have their own code of ethics to not exploit such things for political gain.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The media, both mainstream and alternative, should also exercise ethical judgement in how these are covered.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I find it curious that the Member's suggestion stops at Ministers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The inference I can make from the Member's reference to conflicts of interest in his speech, is that it is because Ministers oversee Ministry budgets and Ministries are involved in procurement tenders.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But let us not forget that all our elected MPs, opposition MPs included, have a part to play in the running of Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, by that rationale, the Member’s suggestion should have extended to all MPs, opposition MPs included.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But in many countries that have such declarations in place, there are problems with evasion, which becomes a political hot point.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The content of the declarations themselves also become political issues.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the assets of Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, which distracts from debate on real national issues like jobs, housing and the economy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, we heard two Ministers explain their housing choices in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To be fair, let us look across the aisle – on my side of the aisle as well – I would not be surprised, given their past careers, that many opposition Members in this House live in private condominiums or landed homes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: When made in declarations, these would also become part of the political debate and perhaps even elections issues.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these people would have already had some success in their careers and understandably, they would have put their hard-earned monies into properties and other investments.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine now asking them to put this all up for public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They are new candidates – there is no question of corruption at that stage because they were private citizens.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think we must be careful when making such suggestions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We should not just pluck and propose without looking at the current system that we have and how effective it already is.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But taking it as it appears to be, I think we should not propose mechanisms that have the effect of politicising the private lives of politicians and in this case, only a particular category.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A budget is allocated to Parliament to carry out its functions with competence.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us ensure that we build an environment where good people are not deterred from entering politics and contributing in this House and in Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Failing to do so will be to the detriment of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their cuts.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Indeed, it is important to have a strong Parliamentary system and a strong Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms He Ting Ru ran through a number of points.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would just say broadly, insofar as the Office of the Speaker is concerned, that is provided for in the Constitution and our legislation.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Speakers in this House have endeavoured to uphold those principles.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where there has been any deviation, that certainly has been addressed.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, the principle of the Speaker's impartiality is not in dispute and certainly, the principle of why the Speaker does not participate in a debate is very similar in many jurisdictions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The system that we have and the way that we organise our Parliamentary business, is actually not very different from many other places.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Each country has its own variations and every country has to adapt for its particular circumstances.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But if we were to ask our people and if we were to ask around Singapore, is there a high level of trust in our Parliament?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: How does Singapore fare compared to Parliaments in other countries?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think you would find Singapore does well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is testimony and credit to the many Speakers who have sat in this House and upheld their duties with dedication and a lot of hard work.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think the other point that Ms He Ting Ru raised was that one must have the ability to properly represent and operate in Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think there is no dispute about that either.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The way our system is structured is that the Government carries out the business of the Executive; and the Legislature or Parliament carries out the business of law-making, of scrutinising Bills, of holding the Ministries and the Ministers to account through Parliamentary Questions, Motions and various other procedural devices.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All of this is available and have been actively deployed, not just by Government MPs, but also MPs from the opposition.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think one other point that Ms He raised was that policy-launching must flow through Parliament first and foremost.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think there may be a misunderstanding here about the role of the Government or the Executive, and the role of the Legislature.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is the role and the duty of the Government to develop policies, to implement them, to operationalise them, to carry it out.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When it comes to making laws, the Government has to bring it before Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parliament can ask questions and hold the Ministers to account.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is a distinction between the two roles and one should be careful not to conflate the two.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our system of having the Executive separate from the Legislature is a well-known, well-tried and tested one.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think the key point that Ms He was making was that Parliament should be accountable, accessible and people must be able to trust our Parliamentarians.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On that point, I agree, which is why it is extremely important that when MPs say something, they should not do so without basis.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Importantly, MPs should not lie to Parliament, nor to Select Committees of Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, it is also important that MPs do not, then, after something has transpired in Parliament, go outside of Parliament and misrepresent what has occurred in Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those things are very important too, for accountability of the MPs and for transparency, and also to maintain trust in MPs.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I move on now to the second point about Parliamentary Committees or Select Committees, which Ms He alluded to, and I think that was essentially the main point of what Mr Gerald Giam raised.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He is essentially saying that in addition to the standing Select Committees that we have, we should create more Select Committees to oversee various Ministries, if that is how I understood him correctly, and that has been done in other countries.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think the question that we have to ask ourselves is, in the other countries where they have these multitudes of Select Committees, are they necessarily better governed?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would venture to say no, not necessarily, to all of those questions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In fact, on many international rankings by any measure, you will find that Singapore fares well in governance, transparency, in lack of corruption, or in low corruption.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where it is discovered, it is dealt with promptly, quickly and decisively.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, it would be unproductive for every Ministry to have to answer to a standing Select Committee.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Setting up a Committee for each Ministry requires significant time.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ministries would also have to expend scarce resources reporting to and preparing answers for their respective Committees.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are resources which could be spent on important policy work.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members will also be keenly aware that our Parliamentary Sittings have grown longer, busier and more frequent.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ministries are spending more time than ever preparing for Parliamentary Sittings.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is a cost to this as it eats into the time that the Ministries have for their policy and other work.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Instead, we convene ad hoc Select Committees where appropriate, for smaller groups of MPs to study and report to Parliament on specific topics, and sometimes, novel issues of national interest.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, you can imagine having many more standing Select Committees, each one to inspect one Ministry that oversees many policy issues would be very costly in terms of opportunity cost as well as the time taken up for the civil servants, the Ministers and the Ministries to do this.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since most of our policy issues are cross-cutting, the value of setting up Ministry-specific committees is also questionable.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What we have is a system that works.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When the Ministries have a policy, it is brought to Parliament, either through a Motion or during the Budget debate, which has a broader overview, or when a specific Act is being passed.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We must remember, a Select Committee is really a mini version of Parliament as a whole.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But here you have everybody that is able to ask questions and participate in debate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, the public does not lose out by this.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In terms of being accessible to the public, that does not actually have much to do with Parliamentary procedure.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That has to do with how MPs conduct themselves in their everyday duties, where they see and speak to their residents, interact with their residents and then bring the issues that are of concern to their residents to this Chamber.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are well-versed with all the concerns of the residents of Clementi.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is how you bring residents' issues to the Chamber and how you make Parliament accessible.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is the work that has to be done on the ground.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will move on to address some of the matters which may have been raised by Mr Raj Joshua Thomas.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, I agree with Mr Thomas that politicians obviously cannot be infallible.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: New candidates, for example, or first-time MPs, will occasionally need some latitude.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But at the end of the day, politicians are human as well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is very important that our MPs must have high standards of integrity.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This applies on both sides of the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Every political party must also have its own code of conduct.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The People's Action Party (PAP) has its rules of prudence and its own way of conducting itself and it will be for the opposition parties to look and see how their members conduct themselves as well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the second point, I echo Mr Thomas' call for us to treat all our MPs with dignity and respect.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think increasingly, what is happening, not just in Singapore but across the world, is that politicians do become targets.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When they become targets, it makes it very difficult for them to carry out their duties.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But it also takes a toll on society, because when it becomes too difficult to do the job as an MP or politician, good people will hesitate to step up.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When good people hesitate to step up, some who are not as good may do so.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then, the system and the society will suffer as a whole.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, it is fine if we want Singapore to be a place where we have robust conversations, robust discourse.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we should try to avoid what we do see sometimes and in other countries – a certain level of nastiness, a certain level of direct personal attacks and more importantly, in some cases, attempting to drag family members in, which really should not be the case, as Mr Thomas touched on.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What does it take to not become a society like that?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What it takes is for good people, decent people, to stand up and to say, "We do not approve of this".

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When something is well done, to say that it is well done; to give encouragement and support where a person, a team, a group or the Government has done something well; to let them know that, "You have done the right thing and you have our support", because that is actually the biggest and the strongest antidote to sniping and harsh comments.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is what makes it worthwhile at the end of the day, to know that you have actually made a difference to people's lives and to communities, and made Singapore a better place.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Together, we can maintain a Parliament that engages in robust but respectful debates, and at the same time, deliver effective outcomes in and out of the Chamber.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I do not think she has established that causality.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am referring to Select Committees in other countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I do not think she has established that causality, that they lead to poorer governance and trust.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because is she saying that they cause the people to trust the Government less, because of the Select Committees?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: No, I am not saying that at all.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What I was responding to is the underlying assumption that always goes with the proposal to have Select Committees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am saying that the processes that we have give a lot of room for the Government and Ministers to be held to account.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I am saying that the system that we have already allows for very good governance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not think that having Select Committees essentially overseeing Ministries or having Ministries reporting to them will improve things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: My reference to other countries was then to say that, when you look at those other countries, they do have Select Committees or their equivalents, but are their outcomes better than ours?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: A second clarification on the point she makes about Select Committees being unproductive and a drag on Government's resources.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: What about the resources used by Government Parliamentary Committees (GPCs)?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: How is the time and resources that Ministries spend answering questions and briefing GPCs justified?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Even more so, given that they are not Parliament organs, but PAP party organs?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are PAP Committees, but they are called "Government Parliamentary Committees" because they come from the party forming the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They were formed, for those who are familiar with its history, back in 1987.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When they were formed, then-Deputy Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong took pains to explain that they were different from Select Committees, which include representation from all parties.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, the role of the GPCs within the party construct is to give feedback to the Ministers and to the Ministries, to enable the Government to do better policy-making.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not the reverse, where the Ministries brief the GPCs or report to the GPCs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ministries can brief GPCs where there is a matter that they need to seek the GPCs' input or views on, but the inputs are given through the Minister, because the GPCs essentially are a party construct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the Pioneer Generation Package is not means-tested.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This was something that the GPC for Finance Chair Mr Liang Eng Hwa strongly advocated for and it was something that was fed back to us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I know that others also give feedback and we take feedback from everyone, but essentially, the GPC framework is the party's way of organising their MPs to give feedback to the Minister.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think just this year, for example, members of the GPC for Communications and Information tabled a Motion on building an inclusive and safe digital society, and members for the GPC for Health filed a Motion on improving mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the role of the GPCs is really for MPs from the governing party to help the Government to do better.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Do GPCs get confidential briefings by Government Ministries that are not made available to opposition Members?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Minister said that GPCs get information through the Minister.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does that mean that civil servants do not brief the GPCs?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ministries may brief a GPC for the Ministry's purposes, if the Ministry wishes to seek feedback or to find out about something which the Ministry is doing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if there is anything which is political, that is really not for the civil servants.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is really for the Minister and the GPCs, because the GPCs come from the same party as the Minister.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Chua, I am afraid we are reaching the end of the guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Unless you have a super, super short clarification.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I figured I should, since Member, Mr Thomas, mentioned my speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I just wanted to clarify with him, if he is suggesting that all Members should make asset declarations and not just Ministers?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And does he think that anyone in this Chamber will try to hide their assets?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I was, essentially, asking why is it that the Member stopped at a certain point, because in the example that he used, the UK, it was not only Ministers who declared their assets, but all members of parliament had to declare their assets.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: So, that was the point that I was making.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: I was not suggesting that this is something that we should do.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In fact, if you look at the gravamen of my speech, it was really to say that it is not something that we need to do, within our system.

speaker: The Chairman
text: With that, can I invite Ms He, if you like, to withdraw the amendment?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Our current Speaker reminded us, upon his election last year, of our own fragility and mortality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: He said that we are all too human, and as individuals we may fail, while rules and institutions, which apply without exception, do not.
